title: Growing alexanders
subtitle: A biennial or short-lived perennial with celery-like flavour harvested in late winter.
excerpt: Alexanders is a tall, umbelliferous plant that produces celery-like stems from late winter into spring. It was a staple in English kitchen gardens before celery became widely grown. The young stems, blanched in situ, are the best part of the plant.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from John Evelyn, Acetaria: A Discourse of Sallets (1699) and William Cobbett, The English Gardener (1829). Modern growing notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). UK native range from Flora of the British Isles (Clapham, Tutin, Warburg, 1952).

glossaryTerms.definition: Excluding light from a growing plant to produce pale, tender, milder-flavoured stems. Done in the garden by tying the stems together and wrapping them, or by placing a pot or collar around the plant. Celery, sea kale, and alexanders are blanched this way to reduce bitterness and improve texture.

content.text: Alexanders (Smyrnium olusatrum) is a native UK coastal plant that was grown in English kitchen gardens for centuries as a celery substitute. It produces in late winter and early spring when little else is available.
in late January improves the stems from sharp and bitter to mild and tender.

Alexanders tolerates partial shade and coastal exposure. It grows well in any well-drained soil. Sow seed in autumn direct into prepared ground, or in pots and plant out in spring. It self-seeds readily once established. It is biennial to short-lived perennial: it flowers and sets seed in its second year and then may die, but self-sown seedlings continue the planting.

In late January, when the stems are 30 to 40 cm tall, gather the stems together and wrap them loosely with paper, fleece, or a cut-down plastic bottle. Exclude light completely. Harvest the blanched stems three to four weeks later, when they are pale yellow and tender.

Without blanching, the young shoots in February and March are usable but bitter. Use them in soups and stews where the bitterness cooks out. The flowerbuds in spring, cut when still tight, are mild and nutty. The seeds, dried, are used as a spice with a flavour between celery seed and pepper.
